title: Across the Universe
full_review:
As conceived and directed by Julie Taymor, "Across the Universe" (Revolution) is a bold undertaking. An attempt to portray and explain the entire decade of the 1960s through the music of the Beatles, the film is highly imaginative and, at times, visually stunning. But its weaknesses are also difficult to overlook.

Essentially, this is a lavish music video impeded by a contrived attempt at storytelling. While the musical and visual elements are often original and striking, the plot is a series of period cliches, resulting in a film at once both spectacular and schizophrenic.

Jude (Jim Sturgess) is a Liverpool dockworker who journeys to the United States to seek his fortune and also his father (Robert Clohessy), a former G.I. unaware of Jude's existence. At Princeton, where he learns his father works as a handyman, Jude meets a rebellious frat brother named Max (Joe Anderson), who has decided to drop out and move to Greenwich Village in New York.

Jude and Max become friends and roommates, renting a ramshackle apartment from Sadie (Dana Fuchs), a singer in the mold of Janis Joplin. Her main musical collaborator is JoJo (Martin Luther McCoy), a guitarist who bears more than a little resemblance to Jimi Hendrix. Also on the scene is former cheerleader turned bohemian, Prudence (T.V. Carpio).

Along with these newfound friends, Jude also discovers Max's sister, Lucy (Evan Rachel Wood), and the two promptly fall in love. The times are tempestuous, however, and it's not long before Max is drafted, Sadie and JoJo have artistic differences and Lucy's political involvement puts a strain on her relationship with Jude.

As the characters' names suggest, there are plenty of inside references for Beatles fans to relish. There are also some enjoyable cameo appearances -- by Bono, Joe Cocker and British comedian Eddie Izzard -- and some remarkably effective set pieces matching imagery with music.

For all their appeal, however, the cast members, many of them newcomers, are enmeshed in a plot that is simply a rehash of familiar rhetoric about the era: The Fifties were repressively conventional; we should all do our own thing; the Vietnam War was a big mistake.

"Across the Universe" also celebrates some aspects of hippie culture that remain morally problematic. These include the use of drugs, cohabitation without marriage and a mocking attitude toward organized religion.

The film contains partial, rear and upper female nudity, cohabitation, a sexual embrace, a disrespectful sequence with a priest, drug use, occasional rough and much crude and crass language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
